newsitem.title: UK: NATWEST MARKETS PLANS STAFF EQUITY SCHEME.
newsitem.headline: NATWEST MARKETS PLANS STAFF EQUITY SCHEME.

text.p: NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of Britain's National Westminster Bank Plc, said on Thursday it planned to introduce an employee equity participation scheme.
A NatWest spokeswoman told Reuters that NatWest staff had been told of the plan, which would be open to all, on Tuesday. But how the plan would be implemented was still to be decided, she added.
Last week NatWest Markets appointed Konrad "Chip" Kruger as chief executive of the troubled investment bank, which in February revealed interest rate options losses totalling 90 million stg.
NatWest Group also restructured it, splitting its treasury, foreign exchange, interest rate trading, money markets and currency options functions into a separate arm called Global Financial Markets.
NatWest group chief executive Derek Wanless had been running the Markets arm since the departure of its former head Martin Owen in the wake of the interest rate options debacle.

By raising the prospect of a scheme designed to make employees think more like shareholders, concerned not only with individual bonuses but also with the overall health of the business, NatWest Markets is attempting to mimic successful U.S. firms.
While any scheme would only apply to NatWest Markets, it would be available to all employees and has so far received "a very positive response", the NatWest Markets spokeswoman said.
She said the plan had been discussed with NatWest Group, adding "more substantive discussions with all interested parties will take place when the proposals have been formed".

But she declined to say if this would involve shareholders, some of whom have expressed disquiet at NatWest's performance and the capital which has been sunk into building the investment banking base.

Asked about the timetable for the proposed scheme, the spokeswoman said NatWest "hopes to have something in place by the end of the year". But the plans, while only in the "philosophical" stage, did not mean NatWest would have to be separately capitalised.

The proposals had, she said, been put forward by Kruger, Gary Holloway, Tom Whelan and Alton Irby. Kruger and Holloway, who were joint heads of the global debt division before Kruger was appointed chief executive, came from U.S. bond firm Greenwich Capital.
NatWest bought Greenwich last year and its senior managers have had a strong influence on reshaping the struggling investment bank's business.
